items: Hi everyone. Before I get into the CMS, I want to give you a quick tour of the language it's built on. It's called Goose. Quick show of hands: who here has fought a borrow checker, or spent a day tuning a garbage collector? Keep that in mind, because Goose takes a different road.
tips: Goose SDK v2026.4. Docs: ~/Documents/goose/goose-sdk/goose-v2026.4-macos-arm64/docs/ (start with index.md and tutorial.md).

items: Goose is a systems language. The pitch is three things. It runs about as fast as C. It has no garbage collector. And it's memory-safe by default. Here's hello world: one function, one print. If you've written C, Rust or Go, this already looks familiar.
tips: It reads like C or Rust: statically typed, with inference, in .goose files. See ~/Documents/goose/goose-sdk/goose-v2026.4-macos-arm64/docs/tutorial.md.
If asked how run is instant
goose run compiles in memory with the bundled TinyCC; goose build hands the C to the system compiler (clang). See ~/Documents/goose/goose-sdk/goose-v2026.4-macos-arm64/docs/command_line.md.

items: So how does it actually build? You start with plain Goose source, in a dot goose file.
The Goose compiler turns your whole program into one C file.
tips: The compiler stages are covered in ~/Documents/goose/goose-sdk/goose-v2026.4-macos-arm64/docs/implementation.md; keep them for the longer talk.

items: Then a normal C compiler, like clang, turns that into a native program. So Goose gets the speed of C for free, and it gets out of the way.
tips: goose run uses the bundled TinyCC for instant runs; goose build uses clang or another system C compiler for an optimized binary.

items: Now the interesting part: memory. Most languages split memory into a stack and a heap. The heap is the messy part. Either a garbage collector cleans it up, or you free it by hand and hope you got it right.
Goose starts from the same picture.
But instead of one stack, it uses stacks, plural.
And it gets rid of the heap completely. Memory is handed out in order, and it's given back the moment a block of code ends. That's the whole model.
tips: Goose uses data stacks with a bump pointer: allocating moves a pointer, leaving a block resets it. See ~/Documents/goose/goose-sdk/goose-v2026.4-macos-arm64/docs/goose_spec.md.

items: Why does that matter? First, allocating is cheap. New data just goes on top of the stack, like adding a plate to a pile.
Second, cleanup is automatic. When a block ends, its memory is gone. There's no collector running in the background, and no pauses.
Third, data never moves. So a reference you hold stays valid. Simpler memory, faster programs, no pauses.
Being safe means the compiler stops whole classes of bugs. If a value might be missing, you have to check it before you use it. No null crashes. And every array access is bounds-checked.
tips: Missing values are written T?, and the compiler makes you handle the empty case.
The optimizer removes many bounds checks it can prove safe (bounds-check elimination).

items: A reference can't outlive the data it points at, so there are no dangling pointers. And threads don't share memory. They pass messages, so there are no data races. All of this is caught at compile time, before your program ever runs.
tips: Threads communicate with queues instead of shared state. See ~/Documents/goose/goose-sdk/goose-v2026.4-macos-arm64/docs/goose_spec.md.

items: Okay, but is it actually fast? These numbers are from the public Goose benchmarks, against C++ and Rust. On the left, anything past one x means Goose wins.
On the right is memory for sixteen million records. Everyday C++, the way most people write it, uses 713 megabytes.
Expert, hand-tuned C++ gets that down to 557.
Safe Rust lands at 593. Same neighborhood.
And Goose does it in 149 megabytes. About a quarter of everyone else. So: fast, and lean.
So naturally I wondered: fast language, fast web server? I built one and load-tested it. On the left is a todo API under load. On the right is how many requests fail.
tips: The user's own goose-bench results, one worker each on the same machine.

items: Flask, a typical Python server, tops out around two and a half thousand requests a second.
Express on Node does about fifty-nine thousand. Flask is now basically flat on the floor.
And Goose does about a hundred and seventy-eight thousand. That's three times Express.
Now let's look at failures at five hundred twelve clients. Flask drops sixty-three to sixty-five percent of requests.
tips: goose-bench results/SUMMARY.md, failed requests with keep-alive.

items: Express drops twenty-one to thirty-four percent.
Goose drops zero. Not one request.
That web server grew into a framework called gweb, and the CMS I'm about to show you is built on it. So here's gweb in a few quick slides.
You write your pages in HTML, and your data code in Goose.
gweb compiles all of it together.
And what comes out is one native binary.
No runtime to install, no node modules folder. You copy one file to a server and run it.
Routing is folders. A folder under app is a route, the same idea as Next.js. Folders in, one binary out.
So what happens when a request comes in?
A browser asks for a page.
Step one, the binary finds the page that matches the URL.
Step two, it loads the data. That's just a normal Goose function, called load, in page dot goose.
Step three, it fills in the template. Anything in curly braces is a Goose expression.
And the finished HTML goes back to the browser.
The key thing: templates are compiled into the binary. So if you typo a field name, the build fails. Your users never see a broken page.
Next, interactivity. Most of a page is just HTML. Only a few parts actually need to react.
Here's a page that's mostly static.
One piece of it is a component: a little counter button.
Click it, and only the number changes. Nothing else on the page gets touched.
One component source becomes two outputs. The server renders the first HTML, so the page shows up instantly. The browser gets a small piece of JavaScript just for that component.
Reactivity is compiled. gweb knows at build time which parts depend on which state, so only what changed updates.
Here's the whole component. One state variable, one function, one button. That at-state is what makes it reactive. If you've used Svelte, this will feel familiar.
And the runtime the browser downloads is about two kilobytes, gzipped. So that's gweb. Now, how does it compare?
tips: Core runtime is 2,131 B gzip per the coordinator brief; not re-measured.

items: I built the same shop site twice: once in gweb, once in Next.js. Same machine, one worker each.
Requests per second. Next.js serves about thirteen and a half thousand.
gweb serves two hundred twenty-three thousand. To be fair, production Node usually runs several workers, so the gap shrinks on a bigger box. But one-for-one, that's the difference.
Memory at idle. Next.js sits at a hundred and five megabytes.
Startup time. Next.js takes about two hundred sixty-seven milliseconds.
And deploy size. Next.js ships three hundred seventy-five megabytes.
gweb ships less than half a megabyte. A fast language gives you a fast, tiny web server.
So that's Goose in a nutshell. It compiles to C, it uses stacks instead of a heap, and it catches memory bugs before your code runs. Now let's look at what I built with it.
